To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
DNA pooling is a useful technique to identify DNA markers for regions in the genome known to harbor QTLs, but that the technique has limited use for the identification of new QTLs.

phenotype-based DNA pooling is unlikely to be successful in identifying QTLs, unless they have large effects on the phenotypes, but that a priori DNA pooling is likely to be a useful tool for identifying new DNA markers in the vicinity of known QTLs.

1) DNA pooling based upon phenotypic segregation can be used to identify DNA markers tightly linked to genes of large effect, and 2) DNA pools constructed from phenotypic data are unlikely to permit comprehensive detection of QTLs with smaller effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with

developing and implementing novel strategies to identify and characterize QTLs, and to integrate QTL mapping with other approaches, such as map-based cloning, to identify the genes responsible for the phenotypic variation.
the development of new strategies for identifying QTLs in complex genomes, and for the subsequent use of such QTLs in plant improvement.
the development and evaluation of methods for the genetic analysis of complex traits in plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

DNA pooling is a useful strategy for QTL mapping when used in conjunction with a priori knowledge of the location of a QTL, and is not a good strategy for QTL discovery in the absence of such knowledge.
phenotype-based DNA pooling has a limited utility in QTL identification, but is useful in QTL validation and marker development.
phenotype-based DNA pooling is not a panacea for the identification of QTLs in segregating populations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DNA pooling strategies, while useful, are not a substitute for QTL mapping.
the use of DNA pooling for QTL mapping is not recommended, but that it is useful in the identification of new markers in regions of the genome that are known to contain QLTs.
the use of DNA pools for QTL mapping in complex traits is unlikely to provide a major advantage over conventional methods, and is not a panacea.
The main takeaway from our work is that
phenotype based DNA pools are not a good strategy for mapping QTLs.
DNA pooling is an excellent tool for identifying DNA markers linked to genes or regions of the genome of interest, but it should not be used to identify QTLs.
DNA pooling for QTL identification will not be as effective as it was for simply-inherited traits and the use of phenotype-based pools is not a good idea.
